blocks.speaker: CLERK OF THE COURT

blocks.text: Members of the jury, you have now heard the 22 charges, alleged offences, upon which you are to try the defendant in this case. They will, I suspect, have become something of a blur to you as they were read out, but there was, as you will appreciate, a common theme. They were offences, and only offences, of murder and attempted murder: seven alleged murders, 15 alleged acts of attempted murders. They all relate to babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You will hear, when Mr Johnson King's Counsel on behalf of the prosecution begins to open the case to you, the facts that give rise to these allegations.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Before that happens, it is very important that I explain to you your role and duties as jurors in this case. In your plastic packs in front of you, there should be a document which is entitled "Your legal responsibilities as a juror". Would you please take it out from the pack? Do you each have one of those? Yes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Good, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask that you are also given a one-and-a-half page document, which I have drawn up, entitled "Jury directions", which goes with this document and with the narrative that I am about to deliver in relation to this document. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There's more than sufficient there. There are more than 14.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Handed)
(Pause)
You each have that document as well. For the moment, please, just listen to what I'm about to say and I will draw your attention to these documents at the appropriate points.

The first thing I wanted to try and do is alleviate, insofar as I'm able to, any anxiety or apprehension you may have about your role as jurors in this case. As I've already said, it may well be that as the counts on the indictment were put to you, you were losing focus and concentration and things were becoming a bit of a blur. That is because your anxiety state will have been heightened by the fact that you've been selected to serve as jurors in this case and you will have apprehension about what is to follow, both in relation to the nature of the case and as your duties in relation to being jurors in this case.

I want to reassure you that juries up and down the country are trying very serious cases, so there are many people who are, unhappily, given the task of performing jury service and trying very serious cases, and what I am about to say to you is said in various forms to all jurors.

Do not be anxious. You will find, as this case proceeds, you soon become acquainted with all the material that you need to be acquainted with, all that is put in front of you, what the issues in the case are and what decisions you have to make.

Ultimately, it can be distilled into two simple propositions: I am the judge of the law, you are the judges of the facts. I deal with all questions of law, I ensure that the trial is conducted according to law and I rule on any issues of law that have to be decided.

You, on the other hand, are the sole judges of the facts. You will decide on the evidence that's placed before you what you accept as being truthful and reliable evidence and what you reject as being untruthful or unreliable, and the conclusions that you draw from all the evidence at the end of the case. So you don't approach this case with any sense of pre-judgment about it: you keep open minds and reach conclusions when you have heard all the evidence and the arguments in relation to the evidence.

That is the sort of process that we all undertake in our daily lives when we have to make decisions. We assess the evidence, the reasons, and then come to a conclusion. All right? So there's no actual mystique and then, applying the directions of law that I will give you, I will tell you what law you need to know, you will reach verdicts in this case. So that will be 22 verdicts, a verdict of guilty or not guilty on each of the charges on the indictment. All right?

So that essentially is direction 1 that you have in your sheet of paper that I have handed you, "Jury directions". You are the sole judges of the facts in the case. I, as the judge of the law, will give you written directions as to the law you need to know in relation to the offences and other legal matters at the end of all the evidence. The law is not complicated in this case, it's very straightforward; it's the facts that are going to require analysis and decisions. All right?

You will try this case -- well, I'll come on to written direction 2 next. Offences of this nature, the alleged murder of babies and attempting to murder babies, is bound to provoke an instinctive reaction of horror. We all have emotions, it is part of our characteristics as a human being. Whilst retaining your knowledge and understanding of human behaviour, you must put your emotions to one side and consider and judge the evidence calmly, rationally, fairly and dispassionately.
I am sure you would do that anyway, but you must bear that in mind at all times.

3. You will try this case on all the evidence placed before you during the trial and your assessment of the evidence and nothing else. The case will inevitably attract a lot of media attention. If you read or hear any reports of the case in the media or from any other source, remember that any report is but a selective part of the proceedings.

You may also read comments made by others about the case over social media forums. I am not saying you are prohibited from using social media, but beware: pay no attention to the reports that you read of the case or the views of others that may be expressed to you. You hear and consider all the evidence in this case and you decide what is relevant and what importance to attach to any piece of evidence and you, of course, and you alone are the only people that have to make any decisions in relation to this case.

4. Do not seek any information from any source or conduct any research over the internet or in any other way about anything or anyone involved in the case. You come to this case, through the process that you've seen undertaken, completely detached from everyone and everything associated with this case. That must remain the situation for the whole of the trial. So you do not conduct any research, nor indeed must you conduct any research about the law or the trial procedures in this case or any of the personalities involved in the case.
As I've said to you, I will give you directions of the law that you need to know and apply in this case -- I reassure you again, it's not complex -- and you will decide this case on, and only
on, all the evidence placed before you in this courtroom and nothing else.

5. Do not talk or communicate in any way, for example by social media or texting, to anyone, including a family member or a friend, who is not a fellow juror in this case about the case or anything to do with it until it is all over.
That is of vital importance because obviously when you are not sitting in this courtroom hearing this case, you will be mixing with family members and friends.

This is going to be a long case so there will be very many opportunities for you to talk to people about this case, particularly when they know, and close family members obviously will know, you're performing jury service in this case.

You must simply say, if they ask to talk to you about it, "I must not talk about this case or anything to do with it". In that way you will not engage in a conversation, nothing will be said to you that may consciously or sub-consciously affect your view about something to do with this case, and you'll appreciate that will be wholly wrong. That person hasn't been here, hearing every word of the evidence like you, has no responsibility in relation to the case, has no part in the case. They're curious, obviously, but you must not satisfy their curiosity, you must simply be very firm and say to them, "I must not talk about this case or anything to do with it".

Now, this is also set out in this document, which I'm not going to ask you to look at now and refer to now, but it sets out these rules as well and the consequences of your breaking the rules. If you break the rule and talk to someone about this case or you conduct any research, then you have actually committed an offence and will be punished, and more to the point the integrity of the case is obviously lost and you could not continue to serve as a juror in this case, indeed the whole trial may be brought to an end and have to be restarted.

I don't want to sound heavy or threatening, but I really want to reinforce, as you will see from this, the importance of your obeying the rules. We pride ourselves in this country on having a fair and just system; it depends upon jurors following the rules. All right?

Whilst you are a jury of 14, which you are at the moment, 12 plus 2, do not even talk to each other about this case. All right? So you will be tempted to talk, particularly when you're waiting to come into court, for argument's sake, about the case and saying, well, that was interesting or that wasn't
interesting or something else. Do not talk to anyone else who is a juror on this case while you remain a jury of 14.

When you become a jury of 12, then you will be able to talk to fellow jurors about the case but only when all other jury members of present, in other words, you are together as a group of 12, and if someone talks about the case everyone else can hear what that juror is saying about it. Do you understand? It's so that you don't form into little groups and that sort of thing, talking about the case. Again it's all to preserve fairness in relation to your role as the decision-makers on the facts in this case.

When the trial is over, number 6, you will know this, I anticipate, from the video -- when the trial is over you may discuss the case with anyone except you must never discuss or reveal what was said or done by you or any jury member when you were engaged in your room deliberating on your verdicts. You carry that with you as long as you are alive. It's a lifetime prohibition on you discussing anything about the discussions that took place in relation to the decisions that you reach or have reached in the case. All right?
I'm taking this slowly and simply and that's why you've got it in writing, so that you can refer to it at any time during the course of this case.

If anyone tries to speak to you during the trial about the case or to seek to influence you, you must tell the court immediately. You will find that the court ushers are your route to me. So anything that crops up, if someone does try to speak to you or seeks to influence you, report it immediately. And if you are not at court you should call the police and, furthermore, do not talk to another juror about what has happened to you. All right? If it happens, you simply tell the usher. Don't tell anyone else.

8. You act as a collective group and ensure that each of you obeys the rules. If, for example, one of you came in, in the morning, and said, "I've just looked up such-and-such on the internet and what we've heard isn't right", that clearly would be a breach of the rules. And if that were to happen, I sincerely hope it doesn't happen, but if it were to happen that must be reported immediately to me. All right? So you're responsible as a group for ensuring you all stick to the rules.
So the court must be told immediately and you don't discuss the matter with anyone else, including fellow jurors. All right?
Now, we know that life goes on outside the courtroom. We all have our private lives and other matters to attend to and no one

knows exactly what is going to happen. Sometimes unexpected events during the course of people's lives -- sometimes someone is taken ill, you may fall ill, we've just had a pandemic where people have been falling ill and we are entering the flu season now where people are likely to succumb to influenza.

If any of you are unwell or something untoward takes place, please don't suffer and come into court and therefore spread the virus or whatever it is that you have. Just alert the jury officer and ring in.
Keep the court informed. Because we will expect each of you to be here, just as I have to be here each day, ready to start when the court starts to sit. So do you.

Because if you're not here we can't start if any one of you is not here. So if something occurs, either personal illness or a family member is taken ill, there's an emergency at home, or something untoward takes place which means you have to give that higher priority than performing jury service and you can't provide cover or make arrangements to cover the situation, then please inform the court. Don't -- and you will have been told this by the jury officer, I'm sure -- fail to turn up and simply say why you're not here.

The court sitting times will normally be between 10.30 and finishing no later than, I hope, 4.15 in the afternoon. That is a long day. It may not seem long to you, but I do assure you if you've been sitting here concentrating literally on every word — there will be a break for lunch -- you will have found you've had a full working day.

There may be some days when we will finish earlier, there may be some days when we finish a little later, but it would have to be very exceptional to go beyond 4.15 in the afternoon for a number of reasons. All right? So plan around that, make arrangements around that commitment, Monday to Friday, being here to deal with the case. If there's going to be a day or a time when we're going to finish early or only going to sit a half day I will let you know as soon as I know about it so that you can fill that gap in and know that you're not here and can do other things. All right?

But the main thing is that there's communication between you and me, each telling the other about any difficulty that anyone may have. But otherwise, here for the trial to proceed according to those court times.
All right?

Finally, number 9. If anything is said or happens that is a cause of real concern to one of your number, which is outside those matters I have already indicated, someone approaching you and saying something to you about the case or someone who is a fellow juror saying something they shouldn't be saying because it's contrary to the rules that are set out, then send me a note as soon as possible.

Bring any other problems to the attention of the court usher as soon as possible, who will pass them on to me, and I will address them. Do not wait, if something arises, until the case is over and say such-and-such happened, or, so-and-so said something and it really worried me, what that person said, because obviously it's too late, the trial is over and I won't be able to deal with it. If it's brought to my attention at the time, I can deal with it and I do deal with problems as they go on and solve them by whatever means are appropriate. All right? But don't leave it until it's all over and then raise it. It's no more that common sense. A great deal, you will find, of what takes place is common sense. That's it.
Now then, "Your legal responsibilities as a juror".

This sets out a lot of what I have said. What I'm going to do is, when we break off shortly for the conventional lunch break, which is between 1.00 and shortly after 2 o'clock, I'm going to ask each of you to read through this document before we resume this afternoon and try and absorb the information. But you should keep these two documents together with you at all times and refer to them. It can be quite useful because if you have a strong family members who says, "You can tell me what the case is about and talk to me", you can show them this, what'll happen to you if you do. You may be parting company from them if you do. You know what I mean by that. All right?

So it is very important that you read those and assimilate the information and refer to it if you need to. As I say, you're going to receive a lot of information and it's helpful for you to have that.

In front of you are screens. Mr Johnson will, when he begins his address, explain to you, as I've said, what this case is about. Again, don't be concerned that you have to retain every piece of information you've been given. Unless you have actually got a form of recording memory or photographic memory, you wouldn't be able to do that. There are very few people who actually do have completely photographic memories. But don't be alarmed about that because the issues will become clear and the evidence will become focused for you. Just listen, assimilate as much as you can. A lot of the evidence is going to be put up on the screen.
You will be having some paper copies, is that right, Mr Johnson, of some documents?
A few paper documents of few documents and iPads.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Exactly. You're going to get iPads.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't know whether any of you use iPads. There are very few people who don't use some form of electronic device now. Mobile phones are essentially computers now that you carry around in your pocket anyway. But this will all be explained to you. Don't be alarmed if you're not very tech savvy. Don't be alarmed that you are going to struggle with it. You won't, I can assure you. We will make sure that everyone is following and understanding what is going on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So a lot of the -- it's digital, in other words, rather than paper. It used to be the case that jurors would have lever arch files in front of them and in this case you'd have very many lever arch files, but it's all going to be digital and you will be taken through that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If you want to make notes on anything, you should have a pen and paper available to you. It's entirely up to you, note taking, whether you want to or not.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I would suggest to you that if there is something that you think is really important that emerges in the course of the evidence, make a headline note of it, just to remind yourself, because you're going to be involved in a lot of events over a prolonged period and at least then you've got a note of it to remind yourself, a form of aide-memoire for when you want to recall it or cross-reference back to it. But do not seek to write down the word of every witness that is put in front of you because it would be impossible and you wouldn't be concentrating on the evidence and absorbing it in the holistic sense, which is very important, you would simply just be trying to make sure you were writing down everything that was said, and you would realise that wouldn't be a fruitful way of approaching your task, or you may not think it would be a fruitful way of approaching your task, and, as the issues become more defined, then some evidence becomes less relevant than other pieces of evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: At the end of the case, you will hear addresses from counsel, putting forward their cases and the evidence upon which they rely in their submissions as to how you should resolve the issues in this case. Then I will summarise the evidence, I will go through it again, identifying points and I'll be able to reference you to points in the evidence as well, but make your own references as well because you're the judges of the facts, I'm not. All right? I will just try to help you in that respect,
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: but I don't help you with the decision-making. That's entirely for you. I help you facilitate it, but I don't influence the decisions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Now, I think, Mr Johnson, unless you want to make a start now, it's entirely up to you, you may want to use the 10 minutes that we've got available.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, I'm happy to make a start.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It will be nice for the jury to hear a different voice as opposed to mine. We'll break off at a convenient moment at around 1 o'clock. I'll let Mr Johnson choose when that is. Then I'll send you away for the lunch break and then we'll continue with his address this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Opening by MR JOHNSON
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Hello, ladies and gentlemen. I'm sure you all know the city of Chester. And on the edge of the city of Chester is a hospital called the Countess of Chester Hospital. It's a busy general hospital and included within the facilities that it provides is a maternity unit. And within the maternity unit is a neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The neonatal unit cares for premature and sick babies. In that sense, it's a hospital like so many others in the UK. But unlike many other hospitals in the UK, and unlike many other neonatal units in the UK, within the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester, a poisoner was at work.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Prior to January 2015, the statistics for the mortality of the babies in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital were comparable to other like units. However, over the next 18 months or so, there was a significant rise in the number of babies who were dying and in the number of serious catastrophic collapses. And this rise was noticed by the consultants working at the Countess of Chester and they searched for a cause.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Their concern was that babies who were dying had deteriorated unexpectedly. Not only that, but when babies seriously collapsed, they didn't respond to appropriate and timely resuscitation. Some other babies who didn't die collapsed dramatically, but then equally dramatically recovered, and their collapses and their recoveries defied the normal experience of the treating doctors.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Usually, a baby's collapse is the unhappy end-point to a process, and it's usually secondary to problems with the heart, with infection, or with dehydration.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Usually, when an intervention is undertaken by the medics, a positive response can be expected. But many of the cases you are going to hear about defied those expectations and norms.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Babies who had not been unstable at all suddenly severely deteriorated. Sometimes babies who had been sick but had then been on the mend suddenly deteriorated for no apparent reason. And having searched for a cause, which they were unable to find, the consultants noticed that the inexplicable collapses and deaths did have one common denominator: the presence of one of the neonatal nurses. That nurse was Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the time that you'll be looking at, ladies and gentlemen, the total nursing staff on the books at the Countess of Chester Hospital numbered anything between about 25 and 30 nurses and about 15 nursery nurses in the neonatal unit. I'm not talking about the hospital in general, I'm talking about the nurses in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a general proposition, the nurses worked either a day shift or a night shift or a combination of the two. As a general rule of thumb, more nurses worked on the day shift on a specific day than would work on the corresponding night shift and therefore there were fewer people around at night.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Parents tended to visit their sick children during the day, not so much at night, and many of the events in this case occurred on the night shifts, although when Lucy Letby was moved on to day shifts at a late stage of the time period, the collapses and deaths moved to the day shifts.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because of the inability of the doctors to find what they believed were genuine medical reasons for the deaths and collapses, the police were called in, and the police commissioned a painstaking review by experienced doctors with no connection to the Countess of Chester Hospital. That review suggests that in that period, between the middle of 2015 and the middle of 2016, somebody in the neonatal unit poisoned two children with insulin.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The prosecution say that the only reasonable conclusion to draw from the evidence you will hear is that somebody poisoned those babies deliberately with insulin. These were no accidents. And if we are right about that -- and it will be for you to say whether we are -- the fact that there were two deliberate poisonings with insulin will help you when you are assessing whether the collapses and the deaths of other children on the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: neonatal unit were because somebody was sabotaging them or whether these were just tragic coincidences.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We say that the collapses and deaths of the 17 children named in the indictment were not naturally occurring tragedies, they were the work -- they were all the work, we say -- of the woman in the dock, who we say was the constant, malevolent presence when things took a turn for the worst for these 17 children.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The babies or the names of the babies who we allege were poisoned with insulin are [Baby F] and [Baby L]. [Baby F] was a twin. He was poisoned in August 2015, a couple of days after he and his twin had been born.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby L] was a twin. He was poisoned in April 2016, a couple of days after he and his twin had been born.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was on duty when both were poisoned and we allege she was the poisoner. And it won't surprise you to know, ladies and gentlemen, that there is a very restricted number of people who could have been the poisoner because entry to a neonatal unit is closely restricted.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I see it's 1 o'clock. I'll leave it there for now, with his Lordship's leave, and give you some more detail once you've had a break.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Certainly, Mr Johnson.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right. There is a start. You'll appreciate there's a lot more to come from Mr Johnson. We'll break off now. Could you be ready, please, to come into court at 2.05, which is just over an hour? It takes time for people to come and go. I'm not suggesting you need that long to take any refreshment you want to take, but it just enables people to have a proper break. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So ready to resume at 2.05. In the meantime, please do read this (indicating) and you'll probably want to read it tonight when you get home, just so you've absorbed all of the information.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Thank you very much.
(The short adjournment)
Yes, jury, please.

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She worked throughout the period --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Throughout the period that you'll be considering, Lucy Letby was working in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester. Prior to her arrest, she was living at an address at 41 Westbourne Road in Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As I think I may have said to you earlier, the doctors and nurses at the Countess of Chester worked on a shift system and inevitably the shifts were different, just to complicate things. But so far as the nurses were concerned, at least, there were nurses both on the neonatal unit but also on the children's
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: ward. And it was the general rule that nurses in those two locations didn't mix on a specific shift. So if a nurse started the shift in the neonatal unit, the norm was that that was where the nurse remained for the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Generally speaking for the nurses, on any given day the day shift started at 7.30 in the morning and the night shift ended at 8 o'clock in the morning. So there was a 30-minute period of time where you had the end of the night shift and the beginning of the day shift, working side by side.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: During that 30-minute period there would be a short general briefing for the day shift coming in, which was then followed by specific handovers of individual patients between specific nurses. So the nurse going off would hand over the patient to the nurse coming on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just to make things slightly more complicated, there were two types of day shift, what was called a short day and a long day. The short day would end some time in the afternoon, the long day shift would end at 8 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it's a 12-hour or if you come on at 7.30, a 12 and a half hour shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When babies were handed over from one shift to the next, the system was that there was a sheet produced, which listed all the babies in the unit and their corresponding designated nurse. I'm sure you've worked it out already. The designated nurse was the nurse who was designated to look after the specific patient.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are, and there were, different grades of nurses. Amongst the nurses who were working day to day in the neonatal unit, most fell into one of four separate bands. At the top were the band 6s. In the middle were the band 5s, although the band 5s were split into two. There were some band 5s had done special training to care for babies in the intensive care unit and some had not and Lucy Letby was a nurse that had done special training.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the bottom of the nursing hierarchy --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)

You probably heard my conversation. They've joined again, all right, we're back on again. I'm not going to spend -- I'm just going to say pause next time. I'm not a tech wizard, but I understand the basics of it, I think.
So the band 4 nurses are at the bottom of the hierarchy and sometimes you'll hear the band 4 nurses referred to as nursery nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Within the hospital records for each of the babies that you're going to hear about there is a section in which the nurses made their records and there was a different section for the doctors to make their records. And so on any specific shift, one of the nurses was designated the shift leader and he or she would inevitably be a band 6 nurse. It was the shift leader who had the responsibility of assigning specific nurses to specific babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if Nurse A was assigned to Patient Z, then Nurse A was recorded as being Patient Z's designated nurse, so whenever you hear that phrase, designated nurse, that's the reason.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The consequences of that are probably so obvious that you don't really need me to explain, but what it meant was that the designated nurse had primary responsibility for the nursing care of Patient Z.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Almost always when we see the nursing records we'll see that the specific patient's records were compiled by the designated nurse, although there is the odd exception. And usually, the administration of medicine and that sort of thing, with the recording of the patient's observations, as they were called, their respiration rate, their breathing rate, their sats, saturation, how much oxygen they've got in their blood, and their heart rate are often recorded by the designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, the neonatal unit itself had four separate rooms. In room 1, that was the ICU, the intensive care unit. Room 2 of the four was the high dependency unit, the HDU, so a level down from intensive care. And rooms 3 and 4 were what were classified as special care rooms, so children that weren't so sick that they needed either intensive or high dependency care. And often, though not invariably, rooms 3 and 4 were being used as, to use a fairly industrial term, I suppose, growing rooms, rooms for premature -- or babies who had been sick but who had recovered, who needed to establish a good feeding routine or regime before they could be discharged home. So babies who had had problems, had recovered, but needed -- just needed to get into a routine before they could safely be allowed home.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: With one or two exceptions, the babies whose cases we'll be considering were in rooms 1 and 2. So that's the nurses and the babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As for the doctors, as I said, they would work different shifts to the nurses and different grades of doctor would work
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: differently. On any given shift, the medical staff, unlike the nurses, would cover both the children's ward and the neonatal unit. So that's the first important distinction.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it follows that doctors who were on duty didn't necessarily, and almost invariably didn't, remain within the neonatal unit throughout a shift. You will know, I'm sure, from your common sense that, broadly speaking, there are three different grades of hospital doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the top of the hierarchy were the consultants, in the middle were the registrars, and at the bottom of the medical hierarchy were the doctors who are known as senior house officers or SHOs.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sometimes the registrars and the house officers are referred to by the stage of their training that they'd reached. So often, after their name, it'll say ST and then a number. ST stands for specialty training, so if your ambition as a young doctor was to be a consultant paediatrician or neonatologist, you would start out as a senior house officer, work your way up to being a registrar, and then in due course hopefully, if your ambitions were achieved, consultant.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So after the names of the doctors, often you'll see ST plus a number, and the number is the number of years that the doctor in question had been doing the specialty training. So the higher the number, in effect, of a registrar or senior house officer, the more experienced the doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As always, there may be exceptions, but generally speaking, from 9 in the morning until 5 in the evening, on any given day, there were paediatric consultants on duty, registrars and senior house officers.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At night, the consultants were on call. Senior doctors would, generally speaking, be at home within a 10-minute journey of the hospital. So at night, generally speaking, it was the registrars who provided the senior medical cover, and a registrar could have anything up to about 11 years of postgraduate training as a paediatrician. So we're not talking about inexperienced doctors. So that's the medical background.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Neither Dr Harkness nor the consultant, Dr Jayaram, had ever seen that sort of skin discolouration, but this proved to be the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: first of a series of similar presentations on the skins of babies who suddenly and catastrophically collapsed at the Countess of Chester Hospital over the succeeding months.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We allege, ladies and gentlemen, that it is, in effect, a hallmark of some of the cases in which Lucy Letby injected air into the bloodstreams of some of these small babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: All the resuscitation techniques which would be expected to bring a baby back to life failed and [Baby A] was pronounced dead at 2 minutes to 9 that evening. He died within 90 minutes of Lucy Letby coming on duty.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Her nursing notes, you can see there on the screen.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: They were recorded by Lucy Letby just before she went off duty from that night shift at just before 8 am on 9 June. She was recorded in her own notes as the only staff member who witnessed the events immediately associated with [Baby A]'s collapse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Harkness, the registrar, says that he was reviewing [Baby A] just before 25 past or 26 past 8 and found that Lucy Letby was holding an oxygen mask to [Baby A]'s face. And after a number of minutes, [Baby A] then appeared pale and was turning blue and his oxygen level dropped.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: What he recorded was:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "An unusual blotchy pattern of well-perfused pink skin over the whole of [Baby A]'s body, coupled with patches of white and blue skin all over his body."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the case was referred to the coroner, a post-mortem examination was carried out by a pathologist, at Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool, and the cause of death was recorded as unascertained at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Two independent paediatricians reviewed the records.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The first was a gentleman called Dr Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans concluded that [Baby A] was a well infant in a satisfactory condition immediately prior to the fatal collapse. You'll see there, noted by Lucy Letby, the top of that page on the screen, "Stable at 8.05".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans suggested that the collapse was consistent with a deliberate injection of air or something else into [Baby A]'s
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: bloodstream a minute or two prior to his collapse. His collapse happened when Lucy Letby was next to him. It wasn't long after the noted timing of the start of the glucose infusion, which of course is something that would have given somebody a legitimate reason to be doing something to the intravenous line going into [Baby A]. So this injection of air went in at about the noted time that Lucy Letby has recorded as giving [Baby A] the intravenous dextrose.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The other prosecution paediatrician, Dr Bohin, agreed that the cause of [Baby A]'s collapse wasn't some natural disease. She too concluded that the most likely reason was a dose of air deliberately put into either the line going into [Baby A]'s belly button or the long line, the second line that was introduced by Dr Harkness, by someone who knew that it would cause significant harm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: An independent pathologist, Dr Andreas Marnerides, described the cause of death as unascertained from a pathologist's point of view, but by that he meant that there was nothing in the findings at autopsy that pointed to a reason for why [Baby A] died and he agreed with the paediatricians that it was reasonable to conclude that air in [Baby A]'s circulation was most likely caused by somebody having injected it through one of the lines.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: An independent radiologist looked at X-rays of [Baby A], including images taken after he'd died, and he concluded that even allowing for post-mortem gases to develop, the pattern he could see in the X-rays was unusual and was consistent with air having been injected to [Baby A]'s bloodstream, what the medics call exogenous air administration.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There were other potential causes, he said, but he said it was consistent with that. And he suggested that in the absence of any other plausible explanation, it was reasonable to conclude that the unusual radiological findings could have been caused by somebody injecting [Baby A] with air.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Another expert called Professor Sally Kinsey is a blood expert and she ruled out as a possibility that [Mother of Babies A & B]'s autoimmune disease could have been significant in the context of [Baby A]'s death. She said:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "The mother's autoimmune problem is associated with different sorts of problems, not this sort of problem. Also, it's not hereditary."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The staff on duty, you'll remember that table I showed you, the staff on duty at the time [Baby A] collapsed were the
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: consultant, Dr Jayaram, registrar Doctors Lambie and Harkness, and Christopher Wood.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nurses, [Nurse A], who was the shift leader, Lucy Letby, Caroline Bennion, Mary Griffiths, with the nursery nurses Lisa Walker and Elizabeth Marshall.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Nursery nurses, as a rule, would have had no business in room number 1. If they were in room number 1 that would be unusual.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It doesn't follow that as a matter of absolute fact that means they couldn't have been responsible, but as I've already shown you, as we see the staffing lists develop in succeeding cases, who was there when things happened? By the third case there was only one constant presence when these unusual life-threatening and often fatal events happened.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was to be more than 3 years before Lucy Letby was arrested and interviewed. The first time was on 4 July 2018, then 11 June 2019, and finally 10 November 2020. She said that she and Melanie Taylor, who you'll remember was the day shift nurse, had given fluids to [Baby A] at the time of the change of shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that once the fluid was connected, it had been maybe -within maybe 5 minutes that [Baby A]'s colour had changed. And Lucy Letby described it as:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Almost a rash appearance, like blotchy red mark on the skin."
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said first that she'd called over Dr Harkness, then that she couldn't remember whether she or Melanie Taylor had called him. When asked what she'd thought at the time, she said that she'd wondered whether the bag of fluid was "not what we thought it was". Well, you'll remember what I've already told you about the insulin poisonings of [Baby F] and [Baby L]. Whether the bag of fluid was "not what we thought it was". That's an interesting turn of phrase that we suggest you may care to carry forward as my explanation of the evidence develops because the experts in the case have concluded that whoever the poisoner was put insulin into the bags of fluid in the case of [Baby F] and [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the interview of 11 June 2019, Lucy Letby said that she was concerned at the time about the line and the fluid. She said that she had asked for all the fluids to be kept from the bag at the end to be checked, but there's no record of her having made such a request.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was put to her by the police officers in the second interview that Nurse Taylor was saying that she, Lucy Letby, had been the one who had administered the fluid with the obvious implication
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: that she was therefore the person who had the opportunity to inject [Baby A] with air.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In this interview she said that she remembered it being the other way round, and this is the first, but certainly not the last, time that there will be a factual dispute about events surrounding the death or serious collapse of a baby who was in close vicinity to Lucy Letby. And the police suggested it straight on that she had administered a dose of air.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Her answer? She said it would have been very hard to push air through the line. She said all nursing staff would be aware of the dangers of a dose of air, an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the November 2020 interview, so the final series of interviews, it was put to Lucy Letby that she had tracked the [family of Babies A & B] on Facebook. She said that she had no memory of having done that, but accepted that if there was evidence from her computer, which there is, it must be right.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, Lucy Letby's interest in the families of the children who we say she attacked is another feature of this case that we will see more of as the evidence emerges. We suggest it is an unusual interest and we will see in due course that on some occasions she searched in quick succession for several of the families whose children's names appear on this indictment.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B], the second child, the elder sister by a minute or two of [Baby A]. If we go back to the indictment, ladies and gentlemen, you'll see [Baby B] is named in count 2. This count is different in one significant respect to any other count in the indictment. You'll see it's one of many allegations of attempted murder, but the dates, you will see, are between 8 June and 11 June. The reason for that is that the events in which we allege Lucy Letby tried to kill [Baby B] happened at about midnight on the 9th into 10 June. I don't know how long ago this practice originated, but the convention when drawing dates in indictments is that you go one day before to one day after. So it's not that we're saying she's done something over a period of 4 days, it is that the event, the specific events happened at about midnight, we can't say for sure, just before or just after midnight, 9 to 10 June. So that's the only respect in which this count differs from others.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B] required some resuscitation at birth, but she recovered quickly and stabilised. She was admitted to nursery 1 in the neonatal unit at 30 minutes of age and she was originally given breathing support by use of a ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Harkness tried to fit a line into her belly button but failed and so he inserted what's called a long line, an intravenous line, through which fluids were successfully provided to [Baby B]. [Baby B] needed more help than [Baby A] with her breathing, but that help was by stages reduced and by 9 June, the day after [Baby A]'s death, she managed periods of independent breathing. All her observations were normal and she was stable.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we come to the night shift of the 9th into 10 June, which of course is the night shift after the death of her brother. [Nurse A], who had been the shift leader the previous night, was given responsibility, she was the designated nurse for [Baby B].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was the designated nurse for two babies in nursery 3, which you'll remember I referred to earlier, rather inelegantly, as the growing rooms.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Shortly before midnight, it was noted that [Baby B]'s blood oxygen levels had fallen to 75%. That's what the doctors refer to as desaturation. The nasal prongs that were giving her additional oxygen were somehow dislodged from her nostrils. So on seeing that, [Nurse A] repositioned [Baby B]'s head and the prongs and [Baby B]'s blood oxygen saturation went up to a normal level. At 5 minutes past midnight, Lucy Letby started a bag of feed called Babiven on [Baby B] with [Nurse A].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Babiven is a type of liquid feed that's given to a child through a line that goes into the circulation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At 16 minutes past midnight, Lucy Letby, even though she wasn't [Baby B]'s designated nurse, took [Baby B]'s blood gases. About 28 hours after [Baby A] had died, at about half past midnight, 30 minutes past midnight on 10 June, the alarms on [Baby B]'s monitor started sounding and [Nurse A] was called over by Lucy Letby to [Baby B]'s incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B] wasn't breathing. An emergency crash call was put out at 00.33, and [Baby B]'s saturations, the amount of oxygen in her circulation, was down to 50%.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was blue, she wasn't breathing, and she was limp.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Nurse A] began resuscitation and she noticed a rapid colour change in [Baby B]'s skin, with purple blotches and white patches all over her body. You've heard that before.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B]'s heart rate dropped. The nursing notes were made by [Nurse A], the designated nurse, and they were written up at about 7.30 the following morning at the end of the shift. In a witness statement she made about 3 years later, she said that she and Lucy Letby had been preparing antibiotics at the time
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B] had collapsed and that neither she nor Lucy Letby were by [Baby B] at the time the alarm sounded.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Lambie, the registrar, had attended and put a tube down [Baby B]'s throat and connected her to a ventilator. [Baby B] recovered quickly and once she'd been resuscitated her heart rate increased, her breathing resumed and she became very lively and required minimal breathing support after that. She was given some fluids, that improved her circulation, and there was a reduction in the skin discolouration by the time [Dr B], the oncall consultant, had arrived.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Subsequent routine blood tests were all normal apart from in one respect a finding which the experts suggest may not be unusual in a child of [Baby B]'s age. Other investigations were normal: the X-rays, brain scan, heart scan. But the consultant, [Dr B], noted that there were loops of gas-filled bowel. The bowel, the intestines, loop in your lower abdomen. And that's a finding that you will hear time and time again in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The remainder of [Baby B]'s clinical course passed without incident apart from three episodes of self-correcting breathing problems, which didn't involve the drop in heart rate, and that was all days later.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby B] improved and she was discharged on 9 July and she mercifully doesn't appear to have suffered any adverse consequences of the severe oxygen starvation that happened to her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The independent experts examined [Baby B]'s case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Evans concluded that [Baby B] was subjected to some form of sabotage before and after midnight on the night of the 9th to 10 June. He thought that [Baby B]'s airways may have been blocked and that she may have received a dose of air into her bloodstream. On balance, he favoured some form of sabotage after midnight.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Bohin thought that an obstruction of [Baby B]'s breathing would cause sudden desaturation and a reduction in heart rate but concluded that that wouldn't account for the skin changes that had been seen. She agreed with Dr Evans that whilst it was possible that [Baby B]'s airway was obstructed, that alone couldn't account for her sudden collapse, and Dr Bohin observed that the sudden onset of this discolouration to the skin, in association with a steep collapse, followed by a relatively quick recovery, is rare and only explicable by her having been given a dose of air into her bloodstream.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's not just the speed of the collapse, ladies and gentlemen, but the speed of the recovery sometimes. And Dr Bohin noted that a bag of fluids had been connected to [Baby B]'s long line at about 00.05 and that that would give the opportunity, or the cover, to someone for deliberate introduction of a dose of air into the bloodstream.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: After all, ladies and gentlemen, the same thing had happened with [Baby A] the night before, hadn't it?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Kinsey, the blood specialist, noted the account of the skin discolouration and she explained that by saying that if air was injected into a vein, it would pass through the circulation to the heart, going into the right side of the heart, which would cause problems with the blood vessels of the lungs. But in a newborn, there is a naturally occurring hole in the heart and that means that air that's injected into a vein can cross from the circulation of the veins into the circulation of the arteries, the circulation going out.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in other words, blood returning to the heart passes straight out again without being oxygenated by the lungs. And that air going in like that would account for the changes in skin colour, as had been described by those who had seen it. But also no blood disorder would account for it, so whilst [Baby B] and [Baby A]'s mum had a blood disorder, the blood disorder could not account for what had been seen.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The staff on duty were the consultant, this time [Dr B], registrar Dr Lambie, the senior house officer Jian Minh Hor, and the nurses Kathryn Percival-Ward, who was the shift leader, [Nurse A], Lucy Letby, Mary Griffiths, with the nursery nurses Lisa Walker and Cheryl Cuthbertson-Taylor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we can already see, ladies and gentlemen, by incident 2, the doctors are different from the previous night. As for the nurses, three of the more senior nurses from the night [Baby A] died were working, and one of the nursery nurses.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When Lucy Letby was interviewed, she was asked about the circumstances surrounding the connection of this bag of liquid, this bag of feed, at 00.05. She looked at some paperwork for what's called a lipid syringe.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: A lipid syringe is a liquid that is added to the total parenteral nutrition bag. It gives you fats that you'd get from milk that you can't get from these bags of total parenteral nutritional Babiven, essentially.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was asked about this prescription and said that it wasn't her writing, but she was the person that had signed for it and that:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Ideally, it should have been co-signed by somebody."

blocks.text: In November 2020, she was asked about a handover sheet relating to [Baby B] that had been found at Lucy Letby's home address during a search. blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So ladies and gentlemen, taking a step back for a moment, it's easy to get sucked in by the detail in this case, but important always to keep a sense of perspective. blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The prosecution's experts say that the collapses and skin mottling were the result of air being injected into their bloodstream. The first injection caused the death of [Baby A]. The second, the dangerous and life-threatening collapse of his sister, [Baby B]. We say that there is no plausible explanation or no plausible alternative to the explanation that this was the result of air being injected into the circulation.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The fact it happened in two cases just over 24 hours apart shows that these were not accidents. Lucy Letby was the only person with [Baby A] at the time he collapsed and she was in the room when the same thing happened to [Baby B], with the records written at the time showing her having treated [Baby B] just before she collapsed. blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON
